questions.question: Let \(A\) be a \(3 \times 3\) matrix with rank \(2\). Then \(AX = 0\) has
questions.explanation: Given that the rank of the \(3 \times 3\) matrix is \(2\), denoted as \(\rho(A_{3 \times 3}) = 2\), and the total number of dimensions (columns) is \(n = 3\). This implies that: \[r = \rho(A_{3 \times 3}) = 2 < n = 3 = \text{number of variables}\] For a homogeneous linear system \(AX = O\), the number of linearly independent solutions is determined by the dimension of its null space (nullity). According to the Rank-Nullity Theorem, it is given by: \[p = n - r\] \[p = 3 - 2 = 1\] \[\boxed{\text{(B) one independent solution}}\]

questions.subject: engineering-mathematics
questions.question: \(f = a_0 x^n + a_1 x^{n-1} y + \dots + a_{n-1} x y^{n-1} + a_n y^n\) where \(a_i\) (\(i = 0\) to \(n\)) are constants then \(x \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} + y \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\) is
questions.explanation:
Given the function: \[f(x, y) = a_{0}x^{n} + a_{1}x^{n-1}y + \dots + a_{n-1}xy^{n-1} + a_{n}y^{n}\] We observe that the sum of the powers of \(x\) and \(y\) in every individual term is exactly equal to \(n\): * First term: \(n + 0 = n\) * Second term: \((n-1) + 1 = n\) * Last term: \(0 + n = n\) Therefore, \(f(x, y)\) is a homogeneous function in \(x\) and \(y\) of degree \(n\). By **Euler's Theorem** for homogeneous functions, if a function \(f(x, y)\) is homogeneous of degree \(n\), then: \[x\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} + y\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = nf\] Thus, the correct option is C. \[\boxed{\text{(c)}\ \ nf}\]
Key points
  • A function \(f(x, y)\) is said to be homogeneous of degree \(n\) if \(f(kx, ky) = k^n f(x, y)\).
  • **Euler's Theorem Statement:** If \(f(x, y)\) is a homogeneous function of degree \(n\), then \(x\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} + y\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = nf\).

questions.subject: engineering-mathematics
questions.question: The value of the integral \(\int_{-1}^{1} \dfrac{1}{x^2} \, dx\) is
questions.explanation:
We need to evaluate the definite integral: \[I = \int_{-1}^{1} \frac{1}{x^2} \, dx\] The integrand \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x^2}\) has an infinite discontinuity at \(x = 0\), which lies within the interval of integration \([-1, 1]\). Therefore, this is an **improper integral of the second kind**. To evaluate it, we must split the integral at the point of discontinuity \(x = 0\): \[I = \int_{-1}^{0} \frac{1}{x^2} \, dx + \int_{0}^{1} \frac{1}{x^2} \, dx\] Let's evaluate each part using limits: \[\int_{0}^{1} \frac{1}{x^2} \, dx = \lim_{t \to 0^+} \int_{t}^{1} x^{-2} \, dx\] \[= \lim_{t \to 0^+} \left[ -\frac{1}{x} \right]_{t}^{1}\] \[= \lim_{t \to 0^+} \left( -1 + \frac{1}{t} \right) = \infty\] Similarly, the first part evaluates to: \[\int_{-1}^{0} \frac{1}{x^2} \, dx = \lim_{t \to 0^-} \int_{-1}^{t} x^{-2} \, dx\] \[= \lim_{t \to 0^-} \left[ -\frac{1}{x} \right]_{-1}^{t}\] \[= \lim_{t \to 0^-} \left( -\frac{1}{t} - 1 \right) = \infty\] Combining both parts: \[I = \infty + \infty = \infty\] Thus, the integral diverges to \(\infty\), making option D the correct answer. \[\boxed{\text{(d)}\ \ \infty}\]
Mistakes to avoid
A common mistake is blindly applying the fundamental theorem of calculus without checking for continuity: \[\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{1}{x^2} \, dx = \left[ -\frac{1}{x} \right]_{-1}^{1} = -1 - \left(-\frac{1}{-1}\right) = -2\] This is incorrect because \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x^2}\) is non-negative everywhere, so its integral over a real interval cannot be negative. Always check for vertical asymptotes inside the integration limits.

questions.question: The general solution of the differential equation \((D^2 - 4D + 4)y = 0,\) is of the form (given \(D=d/dx\)), and \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are constants
questions.explanation: Given the differential equation \[(D^2-4D+4)y = 0\] or equivalently, \[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} - 4\frac{dy}{dx} + 4y = 0\] We need to determine the general solution. The auxiliary equation is \[m^2 - 4m + 4 = 0\] \[(m-2)^2 = 0\] Thus, the characteristic root is repeated: \(m_1 = m_2 = 2.\) For a repeated root \(m=2\), the general solution is \[y = (C_1+C_2x)e^{2x}\] \[y = C_1e^{2x}+C_2xe^{2x}.\] \[\boxed{\text{(C)}\ C_1e^{2x}+C_2xe^{2x}}\]

questions.subject: engineering-mathematics
questions.question: The probability that there are \(53\) Sundays in a randomly chosen leap year is
questions.explanation:
A leap year has \[366=52\times 7+2\] days. Thus, every weekday occurs \(52\) times and two consecutive weekdays occur one extra time. For there to be \(53\) Sundays, Sunday must be one of these two extra days. The first day of the year can be any of the \(7\) weekdays with equal probability. Favorable cases: \[\text{First day = Sunday or Saturday}\] Hence, \[P(53\ \text{Sundays}) = \frac{2}{7}\] \[\boxed{\text{(d) }\frac{2}{7}}\]
Key points
  • A leap year contains \(366\) days \(=52\) weeks \(+2\) days.
  • The two extra consecutive days determine which weekdays occur \(53\) times.
  • Sunday occurs \(53\) times when the extra days include Sunday.

Hence, \[\boxed{(B)\;\left(\frac{V}{R_1},\frac{VR_2}{R_1+R_2}\right)}\]

questions.question: The fundamental period of the sequence\(x[n]=3\sin(1.3\pi n+0.5\pi)+5\sin(1.2\pi n)\) is
questions.explanation:
Given: \[x(n)=3\sin(1.3\pi n+0.5\pi)+5\sin(1.2\pi n)\] \[\omega_1=1.3\pi~\text{rad/sec}, \qquad \omega_2=1.2\pi~\text{rad/sec}\] Fundamental angular frequency is given by, \[\omega_0=\mathrm{HCF}(\omega_1,\omega_2)\] \[\omega_0 = \mathrm{HCF}(1.3\pi,1.2\pi)\] \[\omega_0 = \mathrm{HCF} \left( \frac{13\pi}{10}, \frac{12\pi}{10} \right)\] \[\omega_0 = \frac{\mathrm{HCF}[12\pi,13\pi]} {\mathrm{LCM}[10,10]}\] \[\omega_0=\frac{\pi}{10}~\text{rad/sec}\] \[T_0 = \frac{2\pi}{\omega_0} = \frac{2\pi}{\pi/10} = 20\] Hence, the correct option is (A). (A) 20
Key points
  • Fundamental angular frequency: \[\omega_0=\mathrm{HCF}(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\ldots)\]
  • Fundamental period: \[T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_0}\]

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: Identify the transfer function corresponding to an all-pass filter from the following:
questions.explanation:
Theory: An all-pass filter has a unity magnitude response for all frequencies while introducing only phase variation. For the transfer function\[H(s)=\frac{1-s\tau}{1+s\tau},\]put\[s=j\omega.\]Then\[H(j\omega)=\frac{1-j\omega\tau}{1+j\omega\tau}.\]Hence,\[|H(j\omega)| = \frac{\sqrt{1+\omega^2\tau^2}} {\sqrt{1+\omega^2\tau^2}} =1,\]for all values of \(\omega\). Therefore, this transfer function is an all-pass filter. \[\boxed{\text{ (A) }\displaystyle \frac{1-s\tau}{1+s\tau}}\]
Key points
  • An all-pass filter has unity magnitude response.
  • Only the phase of the signal is modified.
  • Verify the magnitude by substituting \(s=j\omega\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not identify an all-pass filter from its appearance alone.
  • Always check that \(|H(j\omega)|=1\) for all frequencies.
  • Do not confuse an all-pass filter with a low-pass or high-pass filter.

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: A discrete-time system is shown in the figure. The system function \(H(z)\) of the network is given by
questions.explanation:
From the given signal flow graph (SFG), applying Mason's Gain Formula: \[H(z) = \frac{Y(z)}{X(z)} = \frac{\sum P_k \Delta_k}{\Delta}\] 1. Forward Path Gains (\(P_k\)):
  • \(P_1 = -k\)
  • \(P_2 = (1-k^2)z^{-1}\)
2. Individual Loop Gains (\(L_m\)):
  • \(L_1 = k z^{-1}\)
3. Determinant (\(\Delta\)) and Path Determinants (\(\Delta_k\)): \[\Delta = 1 - L_1 = 1 - k z^{-1}\]
  • \(\Delta_1 = 1 - k z^{-1} \quad \text{(Path\)P_1\(does not touch Loop\)L_1\()}\)
  • \(\Delta_2 = 1 \quad \text{(Path\)P_2\(touches Loop\)L_1\()}\)
Substituting the values into the transfer function expression: \[H(z) = \frac{P_1 \Delta_1 + P_2 \Delta_2}{\Delta} = \frac{-k\big(1 - kz^{-1}\big) + (1-k^2)z^{-1}}{1 - kz^{-1}}\] \[= \frac{-k + k^2 z^{-1} + z^{-1} - k^2 z^{-1}}{1 - kz^{-1}} = \frac{-k + z^{-1}}{1 - kz^{-1}}\] D) \(\dfrac{-k+z^{-1}}{1-kz^{-1}}\)

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question:
An analog low-pass filter is needed with the following specifications: Passband:\[0.9\le |H(j\omega)|\le 1,
\qquad
0\le\omega\le2\pi\times1000.\] Stopband: \[|H(j\omega)|\le0.2,
\qquad
|\omega|\ge2\pi\times1500.\]The minimum order \(N\) of the Butterworth filter to approximate the above specifications is
questions.explanation:
Theory: The minimum order of a Butterworth filter is\[N \ge \frac{ \frac12 \log \left( \frac{\frac{1}{\delta_2^2}-1} {\frac{1}{\delta_1^2}-1} \right) } { \log\left(\frac{\Omega_s}{\Omega_p}\right) }.\]From the specifications,\[\delta_1=0.9, \qquad \delta_2=0.2,\]\[\Omega_p=2\pi\times1000, \qquad \Omega_s=2\pi\times1500.\]Hence,\[\frac{\Omega_s}{\Omega_p} = \frac{1500}{1000} = 1.5.\]Therefore,\[N \ge \frac{ \frac12 \log \left( \dfrac{\frac1{0.2^2}-1} {\frac1{0.9^2}-1} \right) } {\log(1.5)} = 5.70.\]Since the filter order must be an integer,\[N_{\min}=6.\]\[\boxed{\text{(A) }6}\]
Key points
  • Use the Butterworth minimum-order formula.
  • Compute the ratio \(\Omega_s/\Omega_p\) before substitution.
  • Always round the order up to the next integer.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not round the computed order to the nearest integer.
  • Use passband and stopband gains correctly.
  • Do not forget that the common factor \(2\pi\) cancels in the frequency ratio.

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: A discrete-time system is shown in the figure. The system function \(H(z)\) of the network is given by
questions.explanation:
Theory: Obtain the intermediate node equation and then express the output in terms of the input. Let the intermediate node be\[W(z).\]From the signal-flow graph,\[W(z) = X(z)+kz^{-1}W(z).\]Hence,\[W(z) = \frac{X(z)} {1-kz^{-1}}.\]The output is\[Y(z) = -kX(z) + (1-k^2)z^{-1}W(z).\]Substituting the expression for \(W(z)\),\[Y(z) = -kX(z) + (1-k^2)z^{-1} \frac{X(z)} {1-kz^{-1}}.\]Therefore,\[\frac{Y(z)}{X(z)} = -k+ \frac{(1-k^2)z^{-1}} {1-kz^{-1}}.\]Taking the LCM,\[H(z) = \frac{ -k(1-kz^{-1}) +(1-k^2)z^{-1} } {1-kz^{-1}}.\]Simplifying,\[H(z) = \frac{-k+z^{-1}} {1-kz^{-1}}.\]Hence,\[\boxed{\text{(D) }\displaystyle \frac{-k+z^{-1}}{1-kz^{-1}}}\]
Key points
  • Write the intermediate-node equation first.
  • Solve for the intermediate variable before obtaining the transfer function.
  • Express the final answer as \(H(z)=Y(z)/X(z)\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not miss the feedback term \(kz^{-1}W(z)\).
  • Combine fractions carefully while simplifying.
  • Ensure the denominator corresponds to the feedback path.

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: Given the discrete-time sequence\[x[n]=\{2,0,-1,-3,4,1,-1\},\]the value of \(X(e^{j\pi})\) is
questions.explanation:
Theory: The DTFT evaluated at \(\omega=\pi\) is obtained by substituting \(e^{-j\pi}=(-1)\). The DTFT is\[X(e^{j\omega}) = \sum_{n=0}^{6}x[n]e^{-j\omega n}.\]At\[\omega=\pi,\]\[e^{-j\pi n}=(-1)^n.\]Hence,\[\begin{aligned} X(e^{j\pi}) &=2(1)+0(-1)-1(1)-3(-1)\\ &\quad+4(1)+1(-1)-1(1)\\ &=2-1+3+4-1-1\\ &=6. \end{aligned}\]Therefore,\[\boxed{\text{(D) }6}\]
Key points
  • At \(\omega=\pi\), \(e^{-j\pi n}=(-1)^n\).
  • Evaluate the DTFT directly using alternating signs.
  • The sequence starts from \(n=0\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not omit the zero-valued sample while assigning powers of \((-1)\).
  • Ensure the sequence indexing starts from \(n=0\).
  • Do not introduce unnecessary factors of \(\pi\) while evaluating the DTFT.

questions.question: The peak value of the output voltage \(V_0\) across the capacitor shown in the figure for a \(230 : 9\) transformer and a \(230\text{ V}\), \(50\text{ Hz}\), input, assuming \(0.7\text{ V}\) diode drop and an ideal transformer, is
questions.explanation: The diode bridge forms a full-wave rectifier. For the ideal transformer, \[\frac{V_1}{V_2} = \frac{N_1}{N_2}.\] Given, \[\frac{230}{V_2} = \frac{230}{9}\] \[\Rightarrow V_2 = 9~\text{V (rms)}.\] The peak secondary voltage is \[V_m = \sqrt{2}\,V_{\mathrm{rms}} = \sqrt{2}\times9 = 12.73~\text{V}.\] In a bridge rectifier, two diodes conduct during each half cycle. Hence, the total diode drop is \(2\times0.7 = 1.4~\text{V}.\) Therefore, the peak voltage across the capacitor is \[V_0 = 12.73-1.4 = 11.33~\text{V}.\] Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{B. }11.33~\text{V}}\]

\[R_{\text{gain}}=10.53\,\text{k}\Omega.\] \[G =\left(1+\frac{2\times100}{10.53}\right)\times10 \approx(1+18.99)\times10 \approx200.\] Thus, the gain changes from \[100 \;\rightarrow\; 200.\] \[\boxed{\text{(c) }100,\;200}\]

questions.question: Notwithstanding overflow, the addition and subtraction of K-bit signed binary number can be realized using One K-bit full adder and
questions.explanation:
• Subtraction can be performed using 2's complement arithmetic: \(A - B = A + \bar B + 1\)

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: An 8-bit 2's complement representation of an integer is FA (Hex). Its decimal equivalent is:
questions.explanation:
Converting the hexadecimal number \((FA)_{16}\) to binary: \[(FA)_{16} = (1111\;1010)_2\] Since the MSB is \(1\), the number is negative in 2's complement representation. To find the magnitude, take the 2's complement of \((11111010)_2\): Using the short trick --- move from right to left, keep bits up to and including the first `1' unchanged, then invert all remaining bits to the left: \[11111010 \xrightarrow{\text{2's complement}} 00000110\] Converting \((00000110)_2\) to decimal: \[(00000110)_2 = 4 + 2 = 6\] Therefore the actual value is \(-6\). \[\boxed{(B)\; -6}\]
Key points
  • Short trick for 2's complement: scan from LSB to MSB, copy all bits up to and including the first `1', then invert all remaining bits. This avoids the two-step invert-then-add process.
  • Hexadecimal to binary conversion: each hex digit maps to exactly 4 bits. \(\text{F} = 1111\), \(\text{A} = 1010\).
  • The 8-bit 2's complement range is \(-128\) to \(+127\); \((FA)_{16} = -6\) lies well within this range.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not interpret \((FA)_{16}\) directly as a positive decimal number \(250\); the MSB being \(1\) in a signed 2's complement representation always means the number is negative.

questions.question:
A microprocessor has an instruction XOR (\(r_1 , r_2\)) , which performs an ExclusiveOR operation of registers \(r_1 , r_2\) and stores the result in \(r_1\). After the following instructions are executed:
XOR (\(r_2 , r_1\))
XOR (\(r_1 , r_2\))
XOR (\(r_2 , r_1\))
Which one of the following is true?
options: Content of register \(r_1\) is half sum of \(r_1\) and \(r_2\)
Content of register \(r_2\) is half sum of \(r_1\) and \(r_2\)
Contents of registers \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) remain unaltered
Contents of registers \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) are swapped
questions.explanation:
Assume \(r_1 = 28\text{H}\) and \(r_2 = 68\text{H}\). Performing the sequence of three XOR operations: Step 1: XOR\((r_2, r_1)\): \[r_1 = 0010\,1000, \quad r_2 = 0110\,1000\] \[r_2 \leftarrow r_2 \oplus r_1 = 0100\,0000\] \[r_2 = 40\text{H}, \quad r_1 = 28\text{H}\] Step 2: XOR\((r_1, r_2)\): \[r_1 = 0010\,1000, \quad r_2 = 0100\,0000\] \[r_1 \leftarrow r_1 \oplus r_2 = 0110\,1000\] \[r_1 = 68\text{H}, \quad r_2 = 40\text{H}\] Step 3: XOR\((r_2, r_1)\): \[r_2 = 0100\,0000, \quad r_1 = 0110\,1000\] \[r_2 \leftarrow r_2 \oplus r_1 = 0010\,1000\] \[r_2 = 28\text{H}, \quad r_1 = 68\text{H}\] After the three XOR operations, \(r_1 = 68\text{H}\) (originally \(r_2\)) and \(r_2 = 28\text{H}\) (originally \(r_1\)) --- the contents of \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) have been swapped without using a temporary register. \[\boxed{(D)\text{ Contents of registers $r_1$ and $r_2$ are swapped}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Track which register is being updated at each step (the first argument is typically the destination); confusing source and destination leads to incorrect intermediate values.

questions.question: The time period of a square wave in the audio frequency range is measured using an 8085 microprocessor by feeding the square wave to one of the four interrupts, namely RST 7.5, RST 6.5, RST 5.5, or INT. The algorithm used starts a timer at the beginning of a time period, stops the timer at the beginning of the next time period and reads the timer values for time measurement. Which of the following interrupts should be selected for this application?
questions.explanation: Time period of a square wave in the audio frequency range is measured by 8085 microprocessor by feeding the square wave to one of the four interrupts RST 7.5, RST 6.5, RST 5.5, or INTR. Since only RST 7.5 is a positive edge triggered inteerupt and other given interrupts are level triggered, so for accuracy in measurement of time period, RST 7.5 should be selected. \[\boxed{(D) \text{ RST 7.5}}\]

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: An 8-bit microcontroller has an external RAM in the memory map from 8000H to 9FFFH. The number of bytes this RAM can store, is
questions.explanation: Given the first location address \(= 8000\text{H}\) and last location address 9FFFH. The size of memory is found using: \[\text{Total locations} = (\text{Last memory location} - \text{First memory location}) + 1 = 9\text{FFFH} - 8000\text{H} +1 = 2000\text{H}\] Converting to decimal, \[(2000)_{16} = (8192)_{10}\] Therefore the RAM can store a total of 8192 bytes. \[\boxed{(C) \; 8192}\]

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: In an 8085 microprocessor, which one of the following is the correct sequence of the machine cycles for the execution of the DCR M instruction?
options: Op-code fetch, memory read, memory write
Op-code fetch, memory write, memory write
questions.explanation:
In DCR M first the opcode is fetched then the content of memory is fetched (i.e. , memory read) , then content is decremented by 1 and again stored in the same memory location (i.e. , memory write).
Opcode fetch cycle=4T
Memory read cycle=3T
Memory write cycle=3T
Total T state=10T
Hence B is the correct option. \[\boxed{(B) \text{ Op-code fetch, memory read, memory write}}\]

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question:
In a 8085 microprocessor, the value of the Stack Pointer (SP) is 2010 H and that of DE register pair is 1234 H before the following code is executed. The value of DE register pair after the following code is executed
LXI H, 0000H
PUSH H
PUSH H
POP B
DADA SP
XCHG
questions.explanation:
Tracing the execution of the 8085 program step by step: LXI H, 0000H:
\[HL = 0000\text{H}\] PUSH H: The content of HL is pushed onto the stack. \[(200F\text{H}) = 00\text{H}, \quad (200E\text{H}) = 00\text{H}\] \[SP \leftarrow 200E\text{H}\] PUSH H: HL is pushed again. \[(200D\text{H}) = 00\text{H}, \quad (200C\text{H}) = 00\text{H}\] \[SP \leftarrow 200C\text{H}\] POP B: The top of the stack is popped into the BC register pair. \[B \leftarrow 00\text{H}, \quad C \leftarrow 00\text{H}\] \[SP \leftarrow 200E\text{H}\] DAD SP: The content of HL is added to SP. \[HL = 0000\text{H} + 200E\text{H} = 200E\text{H}\] XCHG: The contents of the HL and DE register pairs are exchanged. \[HL \leftrightarrow DE\] \[DE = 200E\text{H}, \quad HL = 1234\text{H}\] Thus, after execution, \(HL = 1234,\text{H}\) and \(DE = 200E,\text{H}\). \[\boxed{(A) \text{ 200E H}}\]
Key points
  • PUSH decrements \(SP\) by 2 and stores the register pair at the new stack location, higher byte first.
  • POP retrieves the register pair from the stack and increments \(SP\) by 2.
  • DAD SP adds the value of the stack pointer to the \(HL\) pair.
  • XCHG swaps the contents of \(HL\) and \(DE\) register pairs.

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: A control loop structure is shown in the figure with FC, FT, TC and TT denoting Flow Controller, Flow Transmitter, Temperature Controller and Temperature Transmitter respectively. This loop is an example of
questions.explanation:
In the given control loop configuration:
  • The primary objective is to maintain the temperature inside the jacketed CSTR, monitored by the Temperature Transmitter (TT) and regulated by the Temperature Controller (TC).
  • The output of the Temperature Controller (TC) acts directly as the dynamic set point for the inner loop's Flow Controller (FC).
  • The inner loop consists of the Flow Transmitter (FT) and Flow Controller (FC) regulating the cooling water valve to rapidly suppress flow disturbances before they affect the process temperature.
Since the output of one controller determines the set point of another controller operating in a nested configuration, this scheme is a classic implementation of a Cascade Control system. \[\boxed{\text{(D) Cascade Control}}\]
Key points
Design Objective: The inner loop isolates fast-acting disturbances (like cooling fluid line pressure variations) before they can propagate into the primary process variable.

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: A single stack stepper motor has 4-stator slots and 18 permanent magnet type rotor pole faces. The step size under half stepping scheme is
questions.note: Marks awarded to all (official key: MTA)
questions.explanation:
Given data for the single stack stepper motor:
  • Number of stator slots (phases/stator poles group), \(m = 4\)
  • Number of rotor poles, \(N_r = 18\)
The full-step size (\(\beta\)) for a stepper motor is given by: \[\beta = \frac{360^\circ}{m \times N_r} = \frac{360^\circ}{4 \times 18} = \frac{360^\circ}{72} = 5^\circ\] For a half-stepping scheme, the step angle is halved: \[\beta_{\text{half}} = \frac{\beta}{2} = \frac{5^\circ}{2} = 2.5^\circ\] \(2.5^\circ\) is not listed in the options. \[\boxed{\text{MTA}}\]

questions.ref: Block Diagram and Signal Flow Graph Q1
questions.question: The transfer function of the open loop system \(G(s)\) which is represented by the signal flow graph shown the figure below is
questions.explanation:
Applying Mason's Gain Formula,
  • Forward Path: \(P_1 = G_1 G_2\) with \(\Delta_1 = 1\)
  • Individual Loops: \(L_1 = -G_1 H_1\), \(L_2 = -G_2 H_2\)
\[\Delta = 1 - (L_1 + L_2) = 1 + G_1 H_1 + G_2 H_2\] According to Mason's gain formula, the overall transfer function is: \[T(s) = \frac{C(s)}{R(s)} = \frac{P_1 \Delta_1}{\Delta} = \frac{G_1 G_2}{1 + G_1 H_1 + G_2 H_2}\] \[\boxed{(A) \ \ \dfrac{G_1 G_2}{1 + G_1 H_1 + G_2 H_2}}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: Consider a unity feedback control system whose forward path transfer function \(G(s) = K/s^2\). The steady state error, for a step input is
questions.explanation:
Method 1
\[G(s) = \frac{K}{s^2}\] The error signal in the Laplace domain is given by: \[E(s) = \frac{R(s)}{1 + G(s)H(s)}\] For a unit step input, \(R(s) = \dfrac{1}{s}\). Using the Final Value Theorem, the steady-state error \(e_{ss}\) is calculated as: \[e_{ss} = \lim_{s \to 0} \frac{sR(s)}{1 + G(s)}\] \[e_{ss} = \lim_{s \to 0} \frac{s \cdot \dfrac{1}{s}}{1 + \dfrac{K}{s^2}} = \lim_{s \to 0} \frac{1}{1 + \dfrac{K}{s^2}}\] \[e_{ss} = \frac{1}{1 + \infty} = 0\]
Method 2
Alternatively, we can evaluate the steady-state error using the static error coefficients method : \[K_p = \lim_{s \to 0} G(s)H(s)\] Substituting \(G(s) = \dfrac{K}{s^2}\) and \(H(s) = 1\): \[K_p = \lim_{s \to 0} \frac{K}{s^2} = \infty\] The steady-state error \(e_{ss}\) for a standard unit step input is given by the formula: \[e_{ss} = \frac{1}{1 + K_p}\] Substituting the value of \(K_p = \infty\): \[e_{ss} = \frac{1}{1 + \infty} = 0\]
\[\boxed{(C) \ \ 0}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question:
Common data for Q3.05.2 and Q3.05.3 Given figure shows a closed loop unity feedback system. The controller block has a transfer function denoted by \(G_c(s)\). The controller is cascaded to the plant, which is denoted by \(G_p(s)\).

The transfer function \(G_c(s)\) is
questions.explanation:
The controller block transfer function \(G_c(s)\) can be found using the inverting op-amp configuration: \[G_c(s) = \frac{V_o}{V_{in}} = -A \cdot \frac{Z_f}{Z_1}\] where the pre-amplifier has a gain \(A = -1\). Thus, \(G_c(s) = -\left(-\dfrac{Z_f}{Z_1}\right) = \dfrac{Z_f}{Z_1}\). \[Z_f = 100\,\text{k}\Omega + \frac{1}{10^{-6}s} = 10^5 + \frac{1}{10^{-6}s}\] Substituting the values of \(Z_f\) and \(Z_1\): \[G_c(s) = \frac{10^5 + \dfrac{10^6}{s}}{10^6} = \frac{s + 10}{10s} = \frac{0.1s + 1}{s}\] \[\boxed{(A) \ \ \dfrac{1+0.1s}{s}}\]
Key points
For an inverting amplifier configuration, the ideal voltage transfer function is given by \(-\dfrac{Z_f}{Z_1}\).

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question:
Common data for Q3.05.2 and Q3.05.3 Given figure shows a closed loop unity feedback system. The controller block has a transfer function denoted by \(G_c(s)\). The controller is cascaded to the plant, which is denoted by \(G_p(s)\).

The peak percentage overshoot of the closed loop system is
questions.explanation: The simplified forward path transfer function \(G(s)\) is: \[G(s) = G_c(s)G_p(s) = \left(\frac{0.1s + 1}{s}\right) \left(\frac{1}{(s + 1)(1 + 0.1s)}\right)\] \[G(s) = \frac{1}{s(s + 1)}\] The closed-loop transfer function with unity feedback (\(H(s) = 1\)) is: \[\frac{C(s)}{R(s)} = \frac{G(s)}{1 + G(s)} = \frac{1}{s(s + 1) + 1} = \frac{1}{s^2 + s + 1}\] Comparing this with the standard system equation: \(s^2 + 2\xi\omega_n s + \omega_n^2\) \[\omega_n^2 = 1 \implies \omega_n = 1\,\text{rad/sec}\] \[2\xi\omega_n = 1 \implies \xi = 0.5\] The percentage peak overshoot (\(\% M_p\)) is: \[\% M_p = e^{-\dfrac{\pi\xi}{\sqrt{1 - \xi^2}}} \times 100\%\] \[\% M_p = e^{-\dfrac{0.5\pi}{\sqrt{1 - 0.5^2}}} \times 100\% = 16.3\%\] \[\boxed{(C) \ \ 16.3\%}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: The open loop part of a unity feedback control system \(G(s)\) is unstable and has two poles on the right hand side of the \(s\)-plane. However, the closed loop system is stable. The number of encirclements made by the Nyquist plot of the \((-1,0)\) point in the \(G(s)\) plane is
questions.explanation: The open-loop transfer function has two right-half-plane poles, \(P=2\). Since the closed-loop system is stable, \(Z=0.\) Using the Nyquist stability criterion (clockwise Nyquist contour), \[N=P-Z=2-0=2\] Therefore, the Nyquist plot must encircle the point \((-1,0)\) two times in the clockwise direction. \[\boxed{(A)\;2}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: The asymptotic magnitude Bode plot of an open loop system \(G(s)\) with \(K>0\) and all poles and zeros on the left hand side of the \(s\)-plane is shown in the figure. It is completely symmetric about \(\omega_c\). The minimum absolute phase angle contribution by \(G(s)\) is given by
questions.explanation:
From the Bode magnitude plot,
  • At \(\omega=1\,\text{rad/s}\), the slope changes from \(-40\) to \(-20\,\text{dB/decade}\). Hence, there is a zero at \(\omega=1\) rad/s.
  • At \(\omega=100\,\text{rad/s}\), the slope changes from \(-20\) to \(-40\,\text{dB/decade}\). Hence, there is a pole at \(\omega=100\) rad/s.
Therefore, \[G(s)=\frac{K\left(1+\dfrac{s}{1}\right)} {s^2\left(1+\dfrac{s}{100}\right)}\] The phase angle is: \[\phi(\omega) = -180^\circ +\tan^{-1}\omega -\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\omega}{100}\right)\] Since the plot is symmetric about \(\omega_c\), \[\omega_c=\sqrt{1\times100}=10~\text{rad/s}\] The minimum absolute phase angle occurs at \(\omega=\omega_c\). \[\phi(10) = -180^\circ +\tan^{-1}(10) -\tan^{-1}(0.1) = -180^\circ +84.3^\circ -5.7^\circ = -101.4^\circ\] Hence, the minimum absolute phase angle contribution is, \(|\phi_{\min}|=101.4^\circ\) \[\boxed{(C)\;101.4^\circ}\]
Key points
  • A slope increase of \(20\,\text{dB/decade}\) indicates one zero, while a slope decrease of \(20\,\text{dB/decade}\) indicates one pole.
  • If the Bode magnitude plot is symmetric, the frequency of minimum absolute phase angle is the geometric mean of the break frequencies.

questions.question: A single input single output linear system is described by the equations \[\frac{dx}{dt}=Ax+bu\] \[y=cx+du,\] where \(A\) is an \([n\times n]\) matrix and \(x\) and \(b\) are \([n\times1]\) vectors. The transfer function is given by
questions.explanation:
The state-space model is: \[\dot{x}=Ax+bu\] \[y=cx+du\] Taking the Laplace transform under zero initial conditions, \[sX(s)=AX(s)+bU(s)\] \[(sI-A)X(s)=bU(s)\] \[X(s)=(sI-A)^{-1}bU(s)\] The output is: \[Y(s)=cX(s)+dU(s)
=c(sI-A)^{-1}bU(s)+dU(s)\] Therefore, the transfer function is: \[\frac{Y(s)}{U(s)}
=
c(sI-A)^{-1}b+d\] \[\boxed{(B)\;c(sI-A)^{-1}b+d}\]
